children: 2012 ET - Japanese stocks are higher after Anthropic's IPO paperwork helped ease concerns about a potential AI bubble. Chip-related stocks are leading gains. Tokyo Electron is up 4.5% and Screen Holdings is 5.2% higher. The dollar is at 157.51 yen, compared with Y156.98 as of Monday's Tokyo stock market close. Investors are closely watching quarterly corporate results, with Japan Exchange Group scheduled to announce its earnings later Tuesday. The Nikkei Stock Average is up 1.7% at 63232.37. (kosaku.narioka@wsj.com; @kosakunarioka)

1947 ET - Japanese stocks may rise after Anthropic's IPO paperwork helped alleviate concerns about a potential AI bubble. Nikkei futures are up 1.5% at 63185 on the SGX. The dollar is at 157.54 yen, compared with Y156.98 as of Monday's Tokyo stock market close. Investors are focusing on quarterly corporate earnings, with Japan Exchange Group set to report its results later Tuesday, as the earnings season begins. The Nikkei Stock Average fell 0.8% to 62189.65 on Monday. (kosaku.narioka@wsj.com)

1847 ET - The synergies that Daiichi Life could extract from Challenger may justify it making an improved offer for the Australian annuity provider, UBS analysts say. Having assessed capital and cost synergies, the UBS analysts think the Japanese insurer could lift its offer from 11.80 Australian dollars a share, to between A$12.90 and A$13.30. Even if it doesn't value Challenger's offshore expansion initiative, a range of A$12.40 to A$13.30 looks reasonable, they write in a note. UBS keeps a neutral rating and an A$12.25 target price on the stock. Shares are at A$11.85 ahead of the open. (stuart.condie@wsj.com)

1835 ET - Is the residential property slowdown in southeast Queensland state a cause for concern? UBS poses the question following 1Q updates from Stockland and Mirvac. Both companies signaled softer residential demand. Queensland had previously been a bright spot amidst a weak national market, analyst Solomon Zhang says. UBS highlights a sharp fall in Stockland's Queensland enquiry volumes. There were just 3,700 enquiries in 1Q, down 54% on quarter. "While this turn in momentum is clearly a negative, we do not think conditions are as bleak as feared," UBS says. One reason is that Queensland sales volumes have been more resilient, with 1Q volumes of 627 lots down 25% on quarter. Also, Stockland's enquiry-to-sales conversion ratio of 16.8% in 1Q was the highest level since at least 2019 for Queensland. (david.winning@wsj.com; @dwinningWSJ)

1600 ET - Volatility in Brazilian markets subsides a little from the initial shock triggered by the surprising success of leftist President Lula da Silva's reelection bid. Markets had been counting on his defeat to conservative Flavio Bolsonaro, who promised to trim government spending. But Lula may not be able to spend as freely as in the previous four years. "President Lula's biggest economic challenge is Brazil's public finances," Morningstar DBRS's Michael Heydt writes. "Without fiscal consolidation, interest rates are likely to remain elevated," he says. The iBovespa stock index falls 13%. In early trade, it fell as much as 17%. The Brazilian real weakens 8% against the dollar. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1546 ET - Treasury yields are mixed ahead of Wednesday's Fed meeting. Odds of an interest rate hold are priced at 90%, according to CME. The Treasury auctions $69 billion in two-year notes amid signs of soft demand. September durable goods orders are expected to increase 1.7%, according to a WSJ consensus, after being flat in August. The Conference Board Consumer Confidence Index is forecast to cool slightly. The 10-year yield is unchanged at 4.987%, while the two-year rises 0.032 percentage point to 4.712%. The 30-year slips 0.014 point to 5.300%. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1528 ET - Price pressures in the U.S. might prove more persistent than current core inflation readings suggest, Fitch ratings says. Inflation in the U.S. broadened more clearly than in other advanced economies over the last year, Fitch says. Olu Sonola, head of U.S. Economics at Fitch Ratings, says this suggests the rise in inflation is not solely due to energy. "Even if energy pressures fade, broader price increases could slow inflation's return to target and keep monetary policy higher for longer," Sonola adds. (stephen.nakrosis@wsj.com)

1352 ET - Results of the $69 billion 2-year Treasury auction come in soft, with a final yield 0.3 basis points higher than where bonds were trading in the open market before the bidding deadline, BMO analysts say in a note. That means demand fell short and the Treasury had to offer an extra discount. The 2-year auction stopped at 4.708%. The bid/cover ratio was 2.59 compared to an average of 2.64, according to BMO. The analysts had expected an overall soft result, saying in an earlier note that investors would be skittish ahead of the Federal Reserve's rate-setting meeting this week. (dean.seal@wsj.com)

1230 ET - Investors in bitcoin-holding company Strategy care less about the nearly $21 billion gain on digital assets it recently pre-announced and more about how it will fund future bitcoin purchases, StoneX analyst Mark Palmer says in a research note. The stock will be driven from here by the actions the company takes to strengthen the funding platform that its acquisition strategy depends on, the analyst says. Executives will likely present the quarter as a period in which it constructed a more durable engine for bitcoin accumulation, he says. "The big question that investors will look for management to answer during the company's earnings call is when that engine will be turned back on in earnest," Palmer says. (dean.seal@wsj.com)

1211 ET - Brazilian stocks pare deep losses in the wake of leftist President Lula Da Silva's reelection Sunday. The Ibovespa stock index falls 14%, after being down 17% earlier. A conservative-leaning Congress elected earlier this month is seen as a likely deterrent to Lula's spendthrift ways. "Lula will not have the room to be as antireform as he might have been in the last term," said Steven Schoenfeld, CEO of MarketVector Indexes. Schoenfeld now expects the central bank to hold interest rates unchanged at a hefty 13.75% next week, after five consecutive cuts. The Brazilian real weakens 9% against the dollar. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1202 ET - The European Central Bank remains in its "middle path" for monetary policy that President Christine Lagarde laid out earlier this year, says Konstantin Veit of PIMCO. "While we are currently seeing higher inflation, there are no signs yet that it is becoming embedded," he says. Indirect effects remain contained and second-round effects are not evident. Still, the inflation outlook will be higher in 2027 and 2028 than expected a few months ago, Veit says. The market is pricing around 70 basis points of rate increases, and while risks are skewed toward fewer hikes there is still exceptionally high uncertainty, he says. PIMCO expects policymakers to unanimously decide to keep the ECB's key rate unchanged at 2.5% this week, before hiking in December. (edward.frankl@wsj.com)

1157 ET - The U.K. government is expected to stick within the fiscal rules and keep a credible fiscal outlook, SEB Research's Malte Meuller says in a note. "We expect a relatively modest budget, primarily focused on supporting households and laying the groundwork for future reforms," he says. SEB Research expect the fiscal headroom to be around 10 billion pounds ($13.4 billion) to 15 billion pounds. "This should have limited implications for gilt yields or sterling, as well as for the economy," Meuller says. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)
